title: ‘Analyse’ vs ‘critically analyse’
author: Peter Ellerton
summary: Peter Ellerton takes up a task verb that educators and professionals use constantly and rarely define: the instruction to critically analyse. He first builds a working account of analysis that holds across disciplines, in which one identifies the elements of an object, how they relate, and what purpose they serve. He then traces the word critical back to a root meaning to sift or separate, linking it to criteria and therefore to evaluation. From that etymology he derives three distinct things critical analysis might mean: evaluating the object against established criteria, evaluating someone else's analysis, or evaluating and justifying one's own analytical lens. His practical move is to replace the vague phrase with explicit chains of verbs such as analyse, evaluate, identify, explain and justify, and he illustrates this with three rewritten task prompts. The piece is a compact argument that precision in assessment language produces clarity about what students are actually being asked to do.
points: Ellerton argues that analysis in history and in science share a common core: identifying elements, their relationships and their roles in serving a purpose or function.
The word critical traces to an Indo-European root meaning to sift or separate, which ties it to criteria and so to evaluation.
Critical analysis can mean judging an object against criteria, judging another person's analysis, or justifying one's own analytical lens against alternatives.
He proposes replacing 'critically analyse' with explicit verb chains such as analyse and evaluate, or analyse, identify, explain and justify, and models three rewritten prompts.
quotes: I know this can seem like a pedantic point but I think it's a fundamental problem, particularly when trying to discern between high-level student responses.

I’ve often had it asserted to me that, for example, analysis in history is nothing like analysis in science. My reply to this is why are they both called analysis then? There must be something about the word which can be stretched across these contexts in some meaningful way.

We identify the elements that make it up, consider how those elements are related to each other and their individual role in the overall scheme. We might determine which elements are most significant and why.

Working with a range of people in educational, government and corporate contexts, I have to say that it remains very unclear to me what people mean. Whenever I challenge groups to consider this, it's very rare for a clear and concise definition to be offered.

Another member of this family of words is criteria. Criteria are used to sift or separate, whether by ranking or making categorical distinctions or judgements. And this is interesting because criteria are essential for most acts of evaluation.

To effectively evaluate something, we have to understand what it is that we value about it, and this allows us to construct the criteria for evaluation. So there seems to be a connection between being critical and being evaluative.

In doing so, we would have to explain why our particular analytical lens is useful and perhaps make judgements about the quality of alternative ways of looking at it. By positioning our own approach among others, we situate it and make its value apparent.
Regardless of how one might go about this, breaking it down into such steps offers more clarity than simply asking someone to ‘critically analyse’.
